name: Theophylline
lead: Theophylline (1,3-dimethylxanthine) is a methylxanthine drug that inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors. It is prescribed for chronic asthma, COPD and apnea of prematurity, and occurs naturally in trace amounts in tea, coffee, cocoa and other plants.[1][2] Its first clinical use, in 1902, was as a diuretic, before it was adopted for asthma about two decades later.[1]

In appearance-related discussion it is listed among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history and because it is a close chemical relative of caffeine: the idea is that a diuretic, vasoactive methylxanthine could reduce fluid-related puffiness of the face and eyes, giving a leaner, more defined look. The US label itself records only transient diuresis as a reported adverse reaction, and no published study has tested theophylline for facial puffiness, water retention or other cosmetic outcomes.[3] It has a narrow therapeutic window, and the US label warns that blood levels above 20 mcg/mL are associated with more frequent and severe reactions, including persistent vomiting, arrhythmias and seizures that can be lethal.[3]

paras: The US label indicates theophylline for symptoms and reversible airflow obstruction in chronic asthma and other chronic lung diseases such as emphysema and chronic bronchitis.[3] Wikipedia lists COPD, asthma, apnea of infancy and post-dural puncture headache as main uses, and reference sources describe it as largely a second-line agent today, with inhaled therapies preferred.[1][2]

Beyond bronchodilation, Wikipedia lists increased heart contractility and heart rate, raised blood pressure, increased renal blood flow, anti-inflammatory effects and stimulation of the central nervous system, mainly the respiratory centre in the medulla.[1] The increase in renal blood flow is the basis of its diuretic action; the label notes transient diuresis among reported adverse reactions.[1][3]

Theophylline relaxes airway smooth muscle by competitive, non-selective inhibition of phosphodiesterases, mainly PDE3 and to a lesser extent PDE4, which raises intracellular cAMP; it also antagonises adenosine receptors (A1, A2 and A3 about equally, which accounts for many of its cardiac effects) and has anti-inflammatory actions including inhibition of TNF-alpha and leukotriene synthesis and activation of histone deacetylases.[1][3] The label says its PDE3 inhibition contributes to tachycardia, hypotension and headache.[3]

It is metabolised extensively in the liver, mainly by CYP1A2 through N-demethylation (with CYP2E1 and CYP3A4 also listed), and metabolism combines first-order and saturable pathways, so small changes can produce large shifts in blood level.[1] Smoking speeds metabolism, and drugs that inhibit it such as erythromycin, cimetidine, fluoroquinolones and fluvoxamine raise levels.[1] Wikipedia gives half-lives of about 8 hours in adult non-smokers, 5 hours in smokers, 24 hours in liver impairment and 12 to 24 hours in heart failure.[1] The label gives a bronchodilator range of 5 to 20 mcg/mL.[3]

Theophylline is a dimethyl derivative of xanthine, sharing the purine core of caffeine (1,3,7-trimethylxanthine) and theobromine (3,7-dimethylxanthine).[1][2] Wikipedia notes it is found in tea, coffee, chocolate, yerba mate, guarana and kola nut, usually in trace amounts: brewed tea contains about 1 mg per litre, far below the amounts used therapeutically, and Criollo cocoa beans up to 3.7 mg per gram.[1] The name derives from Thea, a former genus name for tea.[1]

Below peak serum levels of 20 mcg/mL, adverse effects are described as generally mild and caffeine-like: nausea, vomiting, headache, insomnia and transient diuresis. Above that level the label lists persistent vomiting, cardiac arrhythmias and seizures that can be lethal, and warns of extreme caution in peptic ulcer, seizure disorders and arrhythmias.[3] Serious toxicity mainly occurs above 30 mcg/mL according to the label, and chronic overdose in people over 60 carries the highest risk; common features include vomiting, low potassium, high blood sugar and a fast heart rate.[3] Clinicians monitor serum concentrations because of the narrow therapeutic range.[1]

Conditions that reduce clearance and raise risk listed by the label include heart failure, liver disease, fever, hypothyroidism, sepsis and older age; interacting drugs include erythromycin, ciprofloxacin, cimetidine and allopurinol, which raise levels, and rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine and St. John's Wort, which lower them.[3] The label assigns pregnancy category C and notes that the drug passes into breast milk at about the maternal level.[3]

Albrecht Kossel extracted it from tea leaves around 1888; Emil Fischer and Lorenz Ach published a synthesis in 1895, and Wilhelm Traube introduced another method, the Traube purine synthesis, in 1900.[1][2] It was first used clinically as a diuretic in 1902 and reported as an asthma treatment about twenty years later.[1] Wikipedia notes that it was sold as syrup (Theostat 20 and 80) until the 1970s and as Quibron tablets by the early 1980s.[1]

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and appearance contexts
paras: Theophylline appears in appearance discussion mainly as an item in lists of de-puffing or diuretic compounds, alongside caffeine and other methylxanthines. The reasoning proponents give is that methylxanthines increase urine output and blood flow and so might reduce fluid-related puffiness. Wikipedia's article on theophylline mentions the diuretic effect only as the drug's first clinical use in 1902, not as a current use.[1] No cosmetic trials of the drug were found; it is a prescription medicine in the US, so access runs through a prescriber.[1][3]

Registered trials of theophylline address respiratory and other medical conditions, including bronchiectasis,[4] COPD exacerbations,[5] syncope linked to low adenosine,[6] diaphragm dysfunction in critically ill patients[7] and pseudohypoparathyroidism.[8] Older controlled trials examined its effect on acute mountain sickness, sleep in normal subjects, essential tremor, and interactions with the antibiotic clinafloxacin.[9][10][11][12] No study found examined theophylline for facial puffiness or other appearance outcomes.

card.summary: A prescription asthma bronchodilator with diuretic history; nothing tests it for puffiness.
card.note: Narrow therapeutic window; levels above 20 mcg/mL linked to seizures and arrhythmias.

quick.overview:
Theophylline is a prescription drug related to caffeine, used for asthma and COPD. It was first used medically as a diuretic in 1902.

It appears among de-puffing compounds because of that diuretic history. No study has tested it for facial puffiness or appearance.
quick.mechanism: It inhibits phosphodiesterases and blocks adenosine receptors, relaxing airway muscle and affecting the heart and kidneys. It is cleared by liver CYP1A2.
quick.risks: The US label describes a narrow safety margin: nausea, headache and insomnia at lower levels, and arrhythmias, seizures and death at high levels. Many drugs and smoking change its clearance. It is prescription-only.

chain: Methylxanthine with a historical diuretic effect
Proposed: less retained fluid in face and under-eye tissue
angle.text: Theophylline is discussed as a de-puffing agent because it began its medical life as a diuretic and is related to caffeine. It is a prescription bronchodilator, and its appearance use is a proposal rather than a studied indication.
